text: Transformative change and Innovations for Diverse beach Ecosystems and sustainable Livelihoods through Enhanced wrack maNagEment Strategies

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Project goal
To effect transformative change in wrack management globally. Our goal is to reduce conflict, improve transparency in beach management, and help managers align practices with biodiversity and climate goals while sustaining coastal tourism, economic, and community benefits.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Motivation for the project
A significant, yet often overlooked, threat to beach biodiversity is the widespread practice removing wrack (washed-up kelp, seaweed, and seagrass) from beaches. Beach grooming is intended to improve the aesthetic quality of recreational beaches because of the social perception is that beaches should be ‘clean’. Wrack harvesting is removal of wrack for commercial purposes, such as making agar or providing feed in aquaculture.
These practices of removing wrack from beaches impact the natural system:

they remove food and habitat for invertebrate animals that depend on wrack, thereby impacting the survival of larger species such as seabirds
they reduce sand accumulation and dune formation, impacting the ecosystem service of coastal protection from large waves and storm

On the other hand, human activities can also cause excessive wrack accumulation through nutrient enrichment from agriculture and urban runoff. In such cases, beach cleaning may be necessary to reduce eutrophication impacts and can even enhance biodiversity.
A more nuanced understanding of these socio-ecological dynamics is therefore needed to support informed decisions about when beach cleaning is beneficial and when it is harmful to balance ecological, social and economic imperatives.



Wrack is beach-cast kelp, seaweed and seagrass.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Objectives
The project is divided into six work packages that collectively:

Understand how perceptions, cultural norms and governance frameworks shape wrack-related decisions.
Identify which components of beach biodiversity depend on wrack, and how different wrack management regimes affect them.
Assess key ecosystem services linked to wrack (e.g., habitat support, coastal protection, nutrient and carbon cycling) and quantify trade-offs under alternative management options.
Co-develop and test practical interventions that can reconcile biodiversity outcomes with tourism and community needs, and deliver a Best Practice Guide and policy briefs for implementation.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Project goal
To identify focus areas for beach conservation and build local capacity to have ‘beaches for life’ – in terms of biodiversity, human health and wellbeing, and for the long term – in southern and east Africa.
The study region will be used as a test area for developing innovative methods that will be scaled up to continental and global analyses, and the focus areas can be taken up by countries for implementation and further research.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Motivation for the project
Sandy beaches are highly valuable ecosystems that contain a unique biota with high rates of endemism, support the life-history stages of many threatened focal species like shorebirds, turtles, horseshoe crabs, and provide two-thirds of all types of ecosystem services, including food for small-scale fishers, significantly more benefits for mental health than urban parks, and coastal protection against extreme storms and waves.
Unfortunately, high-value sea-facing real estate has been inappropriately developed too close to the shore. Beaches are now lined with seawalls, losing sand to widespread erosion and intense sand mining, and facing rising sea levels and increased storminess that are predicted to accelerate erosion.
This overlooked ecosystem is in a state of largely unnoticed crisis, and urgently needs action for change if we are to achieve the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity goals and targets for beaches, and maintain the benefits we derive from them for current and future generations. But expertise and science in sandy beach conservation to guide decision makers is extremely limited in Africa.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Theory of change
The long-term goal is to have healthy, well-managed sandy beaches throughout the region that are intact, conserve unique biodiversity, contribute substantial ecosystem services to people, and are managed sustainably. This requires expertise in the respective countries in sandy beach ecology and conservation to advise decision-makers, and foundational information on beaches, their threat status, protection level, and where the priorities are for conservation (protection and restoration).
Beaches for Life! will address this by generating foundational knowledge, training a team of scientists per country, establishing a community of practice in beach conservation in southern and east Africa, and bringing those scientists into the global scientific community at the 10th International Sandy Beach Symposium in South Africa in 2027.

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Objectives
1. To develop an ecosystem classification and map for southern and east Africa through field sampling and remote mapping methods
2. To undertake ecosystem threat status assessment and protection level analysis
3. To identify focus areas for conservation of beaches
4. To build capacity and future leaders in sandy beach ecology in southern and east Africa

title: Sandy Beach Science
text:
Conservation impacts
There are four key conservation impacts that this project aims to achieve:

Capacity building: project partners have the equipment, skills and training to do sandy beach ecology
Enduring connectivity: continued collaboration with project partners beyond Beaches for Life!
Conceptual impact: managers understand beaches are ecosystems that need deliberate conservation and sustainable management
Instrumental impact: improved conservation and sustainable management of sandy beaches through development and implementation of new policies and actions

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
text:
When we think about sandy beaches, the picture that usually comes to mind is sun-kissed holidays spent playing in the sand and surf, lying on a colourful beach towel under an umbrella reading or simply staring out at the waves, and cooling off periodically with a dip in the sea.
While you’re doing all that, under your beach towel there are about 70 animals (more in some places, fewer in others) that are buried in the sand. All we generally see is sand and surf, but beaches are living ecosystems, just like forests, reefs and mangroves, with predators and prey in constant pursuit.

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
section: Not all beaches are the same
text:
Not all beaches are the same
Beaches are shaped by sand, waves and tides. This means that unlike most ecosystems that are largely fixed by solid ground, rocks and plants, beaches are dynamic, continually shifting their form through processes of erosion - sand moving off the shore - and accretion - sand accumulating on the shore.



Erosion and accretion are a natural cycles that shape beach ecosystems.


This constant movement of sand on and off the shore is why scientists prefer to define beaches in the context of the littoral active zone - the across-shore zone of sand within which sand is mobile. It comprises the foredunes, intertidal beach, and the surf zone. This distinction is important for how beaches are managed, but we’ll come back to that.



The littoral active zone, comprising the foredunes, beach and surf, is the zone within which sand is mobile.


Even though beaches are dynamic ecosystems, there are still broad types of sandy shores that are recognised, with beaches tending to persist as a single type over time (unless there is a major disruption in the system). These types depend on the tide range, wave climate, and the local sand that get shaped into different forms. Scientists refer to these shore forms as beach morphodynamic types.

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
text:
Beach morphodynamic types
In microtidal climates where the tide range is less than 2 m, waves play a stronger role in shaping the beach than do the tides, and so they are considered to be wave-dominated beaches. In South Africa, all the beaches are microtidal.
Where the sand grain size is fine, the beach is wide and flat. The surf zone is usually wide too, with large waves that lose energy as they tumble through to the shore. These are called dissipative beaches.



Dissipative beaches are wide and flat with fine sand.


Where the sand grain size is coarse, the intertidal beach is narrow and steep. The surf zone is usually narrow too, with waves that break often directly onto the shore, sometimes reflecting their energy back to sea and colliding with the next row of incoming waves. These are called reflective beaches.



Reflective beaches are narrow and steep with coarse sand.


Between these two types are a range of intermediate beaches that have medium-grained sand, and moderate slopes and surf zones. Characteristic features of these beaches are usually well-formed rip currents and/or sand bars in the surf, and cusps - rolling hills of sand - along the shore.



Intermediate beaches usually have rip currents or sand bars in the surf, and cusps on the shore; look carefully to see the cusps on this beach.


As the tide range becomes larger (>2 m) and larger (>4-6 m), beaches respectively become tide modified, and then tide dominated, as the role of tides shaping the shore increases. These kinds of conditions produce ultra-dissipative beaches and mud flats.
Think of the beaches you like to visit - what morphodynamic type do you think it is?

title: Beaches are living ecosystems
text:
The animals under your towel
When visiting the shore, you may have seen some crabs scuttle past, or a few snails crawling where the sand is wet. Although some animals are visible above the sand, most live their lives in the sand, some emerging to swim in the water as the tide comes in. The densities of animals buried in the sand depends on the beach morphodynamic type.
Living on a beach for a small animal (mostly 1 mm to 10 cm) is challenging because the world around them is constantly moving. It’s similar to what it would be like for us to live in a kids’ ball pit that is filled with balls and continually splashed with and submerged in water.



Living on beaches can be challenging if you’re a small animal, like this beach hopper, Africorchestia meridionalis.


If the waves come fast, the animals have very little time to bury themselves. The grain size of the sand can also make that job harder. This is why beach morphodynamics plays such a critical role in shaping beach communities.
On dissipative beaches, the waves gently wash up onto the shore, usually spaced relatively far apart. This gives animals a good amount of time to bury themselves into the fine sand to avoid getting washed away. On reflective beaches, the short time between waves that hit the shore with more force makes it difficult to burrow into the coarse sand before the next wave washes them away.
Because reflective beaches pose harsher conditions for beach animals to survive, the number and types of animals is greater on dissipative beaches than on reflective beaches, and animal abundance and diversity on intermediate beaches falls somewhere in the middle.
Under the average beach towel, you can expect to find around 70 of these animals. But if you take a walk on a dissipative beach, within a 1-m strip of shore from the waves to the dunes, you can find up to 500 000 individuals of a single species!
Visit the Sandy Beaches (s Afr) project on iNaturalist to view some of the beach species that you can find in southern Africa, and Sandy Beach Invertebrates (Global) project to look for beach species found elsewhere in the world.
Next time you go to the beach, see if you can spot some of these interesting animals.

title: Beaches are full of life
text:
If asked to name animals that live on the beach, many would list turtles and perhaps some of the shorebirds - like seagulls, terns, sanderlings and plovers. Indeed, sea turtles lay eggs in carefully dug nests on beaches, and shorebirds feed and nest on beaches too. Although some of these vertebrate animals are found on beaches year-round, many are migratory species that use beaches seasonally. The biggest community of local residents on beaches are made up of invertebrate species - animals without a backbone.



Beaches are important for animals like turtles to complete their lifecycles.


Ranging in size from about 1 mm to 10 cm, there are hoards of macrofauna species that live on beaches year-round. These include surf shrimps, plough snails, clams, mole crabs (sea lice), worms, sand piranhas, beach hoppers, beetles, and roly-polies (pill bugs). Ghost crabs are probably the largely resident invertebrates on most beaches, with adults growing well over 10 cm in size if you include their legs in the measurement.

title: Beaches are full of life
text:
Adaptations for survival
Although it sounds idyllic to live on the beach, when you are such a small animal, each wave is like a tsunami, threatening to wash them out to sea! If they remain on the surface of the sand, it can get incredibly hot in the midday sun (as many of us have experienced!). This is why most beach animals spend the majority of their lives buried in the sand.





Beach animals can burrow with different levels of ease and speed. Among the fastest burrowers are mole crabs (also known as sea lice, although they are actually crabs, not lice). If you’re able to catch one and place it down in the wet sand, it disappears in the blink of an eye. Other species take longer to burrow, like the beetles, sand hoppers, and roly-polies (also known as pill bugs, although they are isopods, not bugs). If the animals live within reach of the waves, and their burrowing time is longer than the time between successive waves, they will be washed away and won’t be able to survive on that particular beach.







Beach animals must have a way to swim, surf, jump, run or crawl. The sand and surf is in constant motion, and beach animals need a way to ‘go with the flow’ to escape predators, and find food and mates. Plough snails use their large foot like a surf board to surf in the swash, and can also it to crawl on wet beach sand. Sand piranhas crawl on the sand, and are very fast swimmers, emerging out the sand to hunt when submerged by the incoming tide. Sand hoppers and pymy mole crickets hop or jump to move around, and ghost crabs can use their many legs to reach top speeds as they run across the shore.







Beach animals need to move with tides. To maintain their relative position on the shore, beach animals need to migrate across the shore with the tides, or else they must live in cycles where they are periodically submerged under water. Plough snails continually surf in the swash to ensure they stay in the dynamic wet edge of the sea. Clams also migrate with the tides, using the vibrations on the shore from breaking waves as a cue to emerge out the sand and surf using their foot, although much less efficiently than the plough snails because a clam’s foot is better suited to burrowing and anchoring in the sand.

title: Beaches are full of life
text:
Very specific habitats
Because beach animals have to be so specialised to deal with the dynamic physical environment around them, they tend to have very specific habitats in which they live. Most species live either on the low shore, midshore, high shore, or above the high-tide mark. They also tend to live on only one or two of the beach morphodynamic types1, and in one or two biogeographic regions.
1 Beach morphodynamic types refers to the different types of beaches that form as a result of the interaction between tides, waves and sand. They range from dissipative, through intermediate, to reflective types on wave-dominated, microtidal shores. Click the link to learn more.This means that many beach animals in South Africa are found only on our west (Southern Benguela), south (Agulhas) or east coasts (Natal-Delagoa), in a specific zone on a subset of the beaches in that region. These very specific habitat requirements makes them susceptible to impacts from a variety of pressures, like coastal development, mining, removing wrack (washed up kelp and seaweed) and pollution because they often can’t survive anywhere else than right where they are.
This also means the responsibility to look after many of the species is entirely up to us in South Africa because these animals occur here and nowhere else on earth.

title: Beach life on the red list
text:
The IUCN maintains a Red List of Species based on assessments of how close a species is to extinction. The assessments allow scientists to categorise species into one of nine categories, depending on whether the species has been assessed, if there is adequate information to complete an assessment, and the level of extinction risk. The collective term for species that are Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable is ‘threatened’.




Categories in the IUCN Red List of Species. Image source: IUCN.

title: Beach life on the red list
section: First ever red list assessments of beach invertebrates
text:
First ever red list assessments of beach invertebrates
Recently, the first ever red list assessments were undertaken for sandy beach invertebrates. There were 20 species that were selected to be assessed. Most of these species occur only in South Africa, some extend into Namibia or Mozambique, and only the four crabs and one clam (Latona madagascariensis) have broader distributions.
A database of species occurrences was compiled from iNaturalist, GBIF, and field sampling to calculate the area of occupancy (AOO1) and extent of occurrence (EOO2) of each of the species using the GeoCAT tool. These metrics, data from past research, and expert knowledge were used to assess the species using the IUCN Red List Criteria and Categories.
1 AOO: The area occupied by a species, calculated using a standard 2x2 km2 grid2 EOO: The total area within which a species occurs, measured as a minimum convex polygon around all localities





Most of the data that helped to plot the species’ distributions and calculate the EOOs and AOOs came from iNaturalist. This is one of the reasons why citizen science initiatives are so important! If you would like to contribute and help make more of these assessments possible, view the citizen science page. Each observation genuinely makes a difference!

title: Beach life on the red list
text:
Species most at risk
Seven of the 20 species assessed are threatened or Near Threatened. The species that are most at risk are the Endangered white mussels (Donax serra), pillbugs (Tylos capensis and Tylos granulatus) and beach ground beetle (Acanthoscelis ruficornis). Click on each of the boxes below to find out why the species are threatened or Near Threatened.
Endangered species






NoteDonax serra










Donax serra (white mussel) is a beach clam that is endemic to Namibia and South Africa. There is evidence of population declines by 50-80% based on commercial catch and catch per unit effort (CPUE) data in South Africa over the past 10 years, disappearance of the species at sites that have been mined in Namibia, and anecdotal evidence of severe declines and/or disappearance of the species at certain beaches in South Africa. Harmful algal blooms can also cause mass mortalities. The overall population is suspected to have declined by over 50% in the past decade and it is therefore assessed as Endangered under Criterion A2.











NoteTylos capensis










Tylos capensis (Cape calloused beach pillbug) is endemic to South Africa. It has a limited range and restricted habitat along the South African south coast, with between 9 and 12 locations extant. It is experiencing ongoing loss, degradation and fragmentation of habitat to expanding coastal development and artificial light at night (ALAN), and has been lost from at least four locations, including inside protected areas. This species broods its young, has small broods and limited connectivity, and has been assessed as being severely fragmented based on the IUCN definition. It therefore qualifies as Endangered under Criterion B.











NoteTylos granulatus










Tylos granulatus (granulated calloused beach pillbug) is restricted to the coast of Namibia and South Africa. It generally occurs in low numbers, and is found in large abundances (hundreds to thousands of individuals) in only a few places. Extirpations have been recorded at the southern end of its range due to coastal development, there are no recent records in the northern part of its range, and it is impacted by mining. Kelp wrack removal takes away an important source of food for this species. Collectively these pressures are causing notable declines in its habitat availability and quality, and declines in the number of mature individuals. This species broods its young, has small broods and limited connectivity, and has been assessed as being severely fragmented based on the IUCN definition. It therefore qualifies as Endangered under Criterion B.











NoteAcanthoscelis ruficornis










Acanthoscelis ruficornis (beach ground beetle) is a southern African endemic species, found only in the supralittoral habitat on sandy beaches along the west coast of South Africa and Namibia. It burrows in the sand or hides under kelp wrack, feeding on invertebrates associated with wrack. Approximately 80% of its recent (since 2000) range is exposed to mining, coastal development and/or kelp wrack removal. These pressures are causing declines in habitat extent, quality, and population abundance, and there is evidence that the species has been lost from some sites that have been mined. The population is inferred to be severely fragmented, comprising small, isolated subpopulations across its range. It is therefore listed as Endangered under Criterion B.





Near Threatened species






NoteAfricorchestia quadrispinosa










Africorchestia quadrispinosa (four-spined sandhopper) is endemic to southern Africa, and is found only on beaches with beach-cast wrack on the south/west coast of South Africa and Namibia. It is experiencing ongoing loss, degradation and fragmentation of habitat to coastal mining, wrack removal and coastal development. This species broods its young, has small broods and limited connectivity. However, where their habitat is intact, subpopulation sizes are large. Therefore, despite limited connectivity, the population does not qualify as severely fragmented based on the IUCN definition. It therefore qualifies as Near Threatened under Criterion B.











NoteCapeorchestia capensis










Capeorchestia capensis (Cape sandhopper) is endemic to South Africa. It has a limited range and is restricted to beaches with wrack along the South African south-west coast. It is experiencing ongoing loss, degradation and fragmentation of habitat to coastal mining, wrack removal and coastal development. This species broods its young, has small broods of 1-9 individuals and limited connectivity. However, where their habitat is intact, subpopulation sizes are large. Therefore, despite limited connectivity, the population does not qualify as severely fragmented based on the IUCN definition. It therefore qualifies as Near Threatened under Criterion B.











NotePachyphaleria capensis










Pachyphaleria capensis (Cape beach darkling beetle) is endemic to southern Africa, and is found only on beaches with beach-cast wrack on the south-west coast of South Africa and along the south to central Namibian coast. It is experiencing ongoing loss, degradation and fragmentation of habitat to coastal mining, wrack removal and coastal development. Not much is known about the species, but it is suspected from the life history that connectivity is limited. However, where their habitat is intact, subpopulation sizes are large. Therefore, despite limited connectivity, the population does not qualify as severely fragmented based on the IUCN definition. It therefore qualifies as Near Threatened under Criterion B.

title: Namibia
text:
Beaches for Life! Namibia (northern trip, left to right): Harhold Beukes (University of Namibia), Gadaffi Muhanze (University of Namibia), Bronwyn van Wyngaardt (Nelson Mandela University), Mayday Haulofu (University of Namibia), Linda Harris (Nelson Mandela University), Anja Kreiner (Namibian Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform), Hayley Brand (Namibia, independent).


The first field trip for Beaches for Life! that was outside of South Africa took place from 7-22 August 2026. Once we arrived at the Sam Nujoma Marine and Coastal Resources Research Centre (SANUMARC) in Henties Bay, it was a privilege to gift an equipment pack to the University of Namibia (UNAM) that includes everything needed to sample sandy shores. The pack also included a few supplies for the related laboratory work, and a copy of The Ecology of Sandy Shores book. We packed the equipment in two 4x4 bakkies, along with food, 200 L of water and more than 300 L of fuel, and set off northwards toward the Cunene River at the border with Angola.



Hand-over of donated sampling equipment and related resources to the University of Namibia.


It took us two days to drive to the northernmost site, camping at Moewe Bay as our half-way mark. It was an interesting introduction to the Skeleton Coast National Park because shortly after setting up camp, we had a visit from the Desert Lion Conservation team. They alerted us to the fact that there were lions in the area, a bit further south of where we were. They said the lions had never come as far north as where we were, and we were likely to be well out of harm’s way, but still needed to be careful. Just in case.





Happily, it was an uneventful stay, and we headed off for a second day of driving. We were aiming to get to Bosluisbaai, just a few kilometers south of the Angolan border, but we were delayed after we got the 4x4s stuck twice in wet sand and mud after miscalculating the route up the coast at Angra Fria. There are no roads to follow north of Moewe Bay, and with the windy conditions in the region, any previous vehicle tracks had long blown over.


We went as far north as we could but by 7:30 pm, we had to settle with where we were because we still had to set up camp and cook dinner over a fire. This mean we sampled at ‘Not Bosluisbaai’ - so named because the is no geographic name or nearby feature by which we could call the site. And ‘St Nowhere’ has already been taken as a place name in this part of the world.



Camping and sampling at Not Bosluisbaai - an otherwise unnamed section of coast in northern Namibia.







Sampling Not Bosluisbaai was a challenge. Because we sample the intertidal beach, we have a window of about 2 h either side of the spring low tide in which we can work. This meant starting sampling in the dark before sunrise - definitely a first for all of us! We collected the samples and data, had lunch, packed up camp and headed to Hoarusib.
Hoarusib is named after the river that is largely underground but does periodically flood. There was evidence of relatively recent flooding, even though the riverbed was dry on the surface. By now, we had started settling into a rhythm. Set up camp, cook food, sleep, wake up before sunrise, make a fire for coffee, sample, have lunch, pack up camp, drive to the next site.
We went back to Moewe Bay, intending to camp at our original campsite. Only this time, it was absolutely covered in fresh lion tracks! To be honest, we were initially stuck somewhere between - this is so cool! and - this is really not safe! We went to check in with the local rangers, who kindly offered us an empty ranger house where we could spend the night.


We also checked in with the Desert Lion Conservation team to advise us regarding sampling the next day. They said they would accompany us, and recommended sampling as late after dawn as we could. We pushed sampling forward by an hour; any later and the transects would have been overrun by the tide and we couldn’t have collected the samples and data we needed.
(For those wondering, yes, none of us had showered since leaving Henties Bay. Although we were in formal accommodation with a shower, there was no water on site, so we stuck with a small bucket of fire-heated water and a cloth.)


When we went to pick up the Desert Lion Conservation team the next morning, they informed us that the lions had moved inland overnight and we would be fine sampling on the beach. It was a difficult beach to sample, with coarse sand and some gravel, but often it’s these atypical sites that provide interesting data!
We packed up camp and drove south to Toscanini - a historically mined site. It was fantastic to find pill bugs (also known as roly-polies), Tylos granulatus, on the beach at night. They are a nocturnal beach species that has been recently assessed as Endangered1.





We enjoyed a final night together around the fire, sampled the next day, and packed up camp for the last time. All of us savoured a shower at our accommodation back in civilisation that night. And although we missed camping out in the desert under the stars, sleeping in a real bed without sand everywhere was a treat.

title: Namibia
text:
Beaches for Life! Namibia (northern trip, left to right): Harhold Beukes (University of Namibia), Gadaffi Muhanze (University of Namibia), Bronwyn van Wyngaardt (Nelson Mandela University), Mayday Haulofu (University of Namibia), Linda Harris (Nelson Mandela University), Anja Kreiner (Namibian Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform), Hayley Brand (Namibia, independent).


The first field trip for Beaches for Life! that was outside of South Africa took place from 7-22 August 2026. Once we arrived at the Sam Nujoma Marine and Coastal Resources Research Centre (SANUMARC) in Henties Bay, it was a privilege to gift an equipment pack to the University of Namibia (UNAM) that includes everything needed to sample sandy shores. The pack also included a few supplies for the related laboratory work, and a copy of The Ecology of Sandy Shores book. We packed the equipment in two 4x4 bakkies, along with food, 200 L of water and more than 300 L of fuel, and set off northwards toward the Cunene River at the border with Angola.



Hand-over of donated sampling equipment and related resources to the University of Namibia.


It took us two days to drive to the northernmost site, camping at Moewe Bay as our half-way mark. It was an interesting introduction to the Skeleton Coast National Park because shortly after setting up camp, we had a visit from the Desert Lion Conservation team. They alerted us to the fact that there were lions in the area, a bit further south of where we were. They said the lions had never come as far north as where we were, and we were likely to be well out of harm’s way, but still needed to be careful. Just in case.





Happily, it was an uneventful stay, and we headed off for a second day of driving. We were aiming to get to Bosluisbaai, just a few kilometers south of the Angolan border, but we were delayed after we got the 4x4s stuck twice in wet sand and mud after miscalculating the route up the coast at Angra Fria. There are no roads to follow north of Moewe Bay, and with the windy conditions in the region, any previous vehicle tracks had long blown over.


We went as far north as we could but by 7:30 pm, we had to settle with where we were because we still had to set up camp and cook dinner over a fire. This mean we sampled at ‘Not Bosluisbaai’ - so named because the is no geographic name or nearby feature by which we could call the site. And ‘St Nowhere’ has already been taken as a place name in this part of the world.



Camping and sampling at Not Bosluisbaai - an otherwise unnamed section of coast in northern Namibia.







Sampling Not Bosluisbaai was a challenge. Because we sample the intertidal beach, we have a window of about 2 h either side of the spring low tide in which we can work. This meant starting sampling in the dark before sunrise - definitely a first for all of us! We collected the samples and data, had lunch, packed up camp and headed to Hoarusib.
Hoarusib is named after the river that is largely underground but does periodically flood. There was evidence of relatively recent flooding, even though the riverbed was dry on the surface. By now, we had started settling into a rhythm. Set up camp, cook food, sleep, wake up before sunrise, make a fire for coffee, sample, have lunch, pack up camp, drive to the next site.
We went back to Moewe Bay, intending to camp at our original campsite. Only this time, it was absolutely covered in fresh lion tracks! To be honest, we were initially stuck somewhere between - this is so cool! and - this is really not safe! We went to check in with the local rangers, who kindly offered us an empty ranger house where we could spend the night.


We also checked in with the Desert Lion Conservation team to advise us regarding sampling the next day. They said they would accompany us, and recommended sampling as late after dawn as we could. We pushed sampling forward by an hour; any later and the transects would have been overrun by the tide and we couldn’t have collected the samples and data we needed.
(For those wondering, yes, none of us had showered since leaving Henties Bay. Although we were in formal accommodation with a shower, there was no water on site, so we stuck with a small bucket of fire-heated water and a cloth.)


When we went to pick up the Desert Lion Conservation team the next morning, they informed us that the lions had moved inland overnight and we would be fine sampling on the beach. It was a difficult beach to sample, with coarse sand and some gravel, but often it’s these atypical sites that provide interesting data!

And although we missed camping out in the desert under the stars, sleeping in a real bed without sand everywhere was a treat.

title: Namibia
text:
Sampling urban beaches
It was a real change of pace sampling an urban beach at Swakopmund, where the intent was to pick up some contrasts with the pristine sites we’d been sampling in the Skeleton Coast National Park. The impacts were evident, with lots of sampling stations containing no animals. The surf was also wild, leaving us wondering if beach sampling could be classified as an extreme sport!



Our team provided lunch-time entertainment for beach visitors at Swakopmund as we negotiated the large, plunging breakers.


We then started the southern leg of the trip. We decided to drive around the dunes to get to Lüderitz rather than driving along the shore and squeezing in an extra site. The desert sand dunes are incredibly large in this region, and are pressed right up against the shore, creating challenging driving conditions. We over-nighted in Windhoek, and headed off to Lüderitz the next day.
We sampled Agate Beach in the northern part of Lüderitz. It was a valuable site to add because it is in a different bioregion to the northern sites. Sampling here allowed us to get some insights into the beach biogeographic patterns in Namibia, and provides the opportunity to make some comparisons with beaches in the same bioregion in South Africa. After sampling, we spent the night in Keetmanshoop, before heading back to Henties Bay the following day.



Beaches for Life! Namibia (southern trip, left to right): Linda Harris (Nelson Mandela University), Bronwyn van Wyngaardt (Nelson Mandela University), Mayday Haulofu (University of Namibia), Gadaffi Muhanze (University of Namibia), Michael Mateus (University of Namibia, back).

title: Namibia
text:
Identifying the animals we caught
With the fieldwork completed, we spent some time in the laboratory at SANUMARC. We did some training on sandy beach invertebrate classification, and worked on identifying the specimens we collected in the field. We made some interesting discoveries, finding new range limits for some species, and noting others that are likely undescribed species.



Lab work at SANUMARC where we spent time identifying some of the invertebrates we collected, such as the beach hoppers, Africorchestia skoogi (top) and Africorchestia quadrispinosa (bottom).

title: Namibia
text:
Next steps
The site data from the beaches we sampled are currently being compiled into a dataset that will inform the beach ecosystem classification and mapping (project objective 1). Although biodiversity is not an explicit objective in Beaches for Life!, it is essential capacity building for Namibia to advance sandy beach ecological research in future (project objective 4). We can also use the biodiversity information to validate some of the desktop-based analyses of ecological condition (project objective 2) and add any key information for the site prioritisation (project objective 3).
We have subsequently had a follow-up online training workshop on science writing with Namibia and South African students assisting in the project. Our findings on beach biodiversity in Namibia will be documented in a publication that we are currently working on, led by Mayday Haulofu, who will also present this work at the 10th International Sandy Beach Symposium in June 2027. We have started applying for funding to support some follow-up transboundary research, and it has also been wonderful to see the donated equipment being used in subsequent student practicals at UNAM.
We are grateful to the Pew Charitable Trusts for making this work possible.



Namibia has an interesting coastline where sandy beaches blend seamlessly into adjacent desert systems, providing a unique case of a country with primarily pristine natural shores. These conditions in the north contrast with heavily impacted, mined beaches in the south.

title: Citizen science
text:
If you have ever wanted to contribute to research and conservation, this is your chance! There are several citizen science projects on iNaturalist that you can join. It’s the perfect excuse to go to the beach!
Think of it as Instagram for nature. Go to the beach, take pictures of any plants or animals that you can find with the GPS of your phone turned on, post the pictures to the iNaturalist app (on the Apple and Play Stores) or the iNaturalist website, use the AI suggestions for the identification or give it your best guess, and you’re done. Other people will help to identify what you saw, and when enough people agree, the observation gets recorded as ‘Research Grade’.
You never know, you might just have found a species that no one knows about yet. Or found a species where it hasn’t previously been recorded. All observations count!
There are three beach projects you can contribute to…

1. Sandy Beaches (s Afr)


This project includes all observations of sandy beach macrofauna - the insects, crabs, snails, clams, sand piranhas, worms and other small invertebrate animals on beaches in southern Africa. Most of these species have very limited distributions and are often found in one bioregion, and no where else in the world! The best places to look for these animals is where the sand is wet on the beach, and under washed-up kelp, seaweed and damp driftwood.




    Latest observations. Explore all observations at
    
      Sandy Beaches (s Afr) »
    
  




2. Seashore Vegetation (s Afr)

 Dunes are the most sensitive component of sandy shores. The plants that grow on dunes are highly specialised, with pioneer species helping to bind sand together and promote dune formation. Dune plants sometimes require a salt crust on the surface of the sand so they can establish themselves and grow. The salt crust breaks when people walk on dunes, so if you’re taking pictures of dune plants, try to keep off the dune itself to protect these important plants.




    Latest observations. Explore all observations at
    
      Seashore Vegetation (s Afr) »
    
  




3. Ghost Crab Watch (s Afr)


With climate change, many species are shifting their ranges to move into climatic conditions that have become suitable for them, or move away from areas that are no longer suitable. Beach animals only have one choice - to move along the shore, so it’s reasonably easy to track shifts in their ranges. Ghost crabs are expanding their ranges along the South African south coast as the Agulhas Current warms, and the baby crabs are able to survive the cold winters.

      Ghost Crab Watch (s Afr) »

title: Publications
text:
The first red list assessments of sandy beach ecosystem types and invertebrate species, globally. In South Africa, 3 of 12 beach ecosystem types are Endangered, and 4 of 20 species assessed are Endangered. Key pressures are mining, coastal development, artificial light at night, and wrack removal.
Read more








Beaches provide important benefits to people, delivering two-thirds of all types of recognised ecosystem services, including every type of cultural service. All components of the littoral active zone (dunes, beach, surf) are important for delivering services in 11 ecosystem service bundles.
Read more








As ecotonal ecosystems at the land-sea interface, beaches are often poorly represented in ecosystem maps. We define a seashore zone from the dune base - as a proxy for the decadal scale high water mark - to the back of the surf zone, using remote methods to map ecosystem types therein.
